events.title: Apache Cassandra open sourced
events.summary: Facebook released Cassandra as open source on July 14, 2008 — a distributed wide-column database inspired by Amazon Dynamo and Google Bigtable.
events.about: Cassandra trades joins for linear scalability: data is partitioned across a ring of nodes with tunable consistency. Facebook built it for inbox search; Netflix, Apple, and Discord later ran it for massive write-heavy workloads. It joined the Apache Incubator in 2009 and graduated as a top-level project in 2010 — a flagship NoSQL option beside MongoDB and Redis.

narrative.whyChosen: Cassandra brought Facebook-scale distributed storage patterns to the open-source world.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved wide-column NoSQL could run in production at billion-row scale with no single point of failure.
narrative.problemSolved: Web-scale apps needed always-on storage that survived node and datacenter failures without a central master.

events.title: iPhone App Store opens
events.summary: Apple opened the App Store on July 10, 2008 — letting third-party developers sell native iPhone apps to consumers.
events.about: The App Store turned the iPhone from a phone with a browser into a platform — Objective-C and later Swift SDKs, in-app purchases, and review gates. Indie developers and startups built businesses on mobile apps; 'there's an app for that' became the default UX pattern. Android Market (later Google Play) followed the same model.

narrative.whyChosen: The App Store invented mainstream mobile app distribution and monetization.
narrative.whyImportant: It created the native mobile developer career path and app economy alongside the web.
narrative.problemSolved: Early iPhones had no sanctioned way for developers to ship software to users at scale.

events.title: iPhone 3G released
events.summary: Apple began selling the iPhone 3G on July 11, 2008 — adding 3G cellular data and launching in 22 countries alongside the App Store.
events.about: The iPhone 3G made mobile broadband practical — web apps and native App Store downloads over cellular replaced EDGE trickle speeds. GPS enabled location-based services developers still build on. The simultaneous App Store launch turned the 3G into the first iPhone that was both fast on the network and open to third-party software at scale.

narrative.whyChosen: The iPhone 3G paired 3G networking with the App Store's global rollout.
narrative.whyImportant: It made mobile web and app experiences viable over cellular, not just Wi-Fi.
narrative.problemSolved: The original iPhone's EDGE network was too slow for rich mobile web and app downloads.
